data.name: Prove the total and ratio
data.narration: Twelve pounds plus eighteen pounds gives thirty pounds. And twelve to eighteen simplifies to two to three. Both tests agree.
data.caption: Both checks agree!

p.label: Y7-059 · Share thirty pounds
p.context: Ava and Ben share thirty pounds in the ratio two to three.

steps.name: Deal counters into ratio groups
steps.narration: The ratio two to three tells us to make two equal parts for Ava and three equal parts for Ben. These are parts, not pounds yet.
steps.caption: Count the parts first!

steps.name: Build the equal-part bar
steps.narration: Every outlined box stands for the same quantity. Ava gets two boxes and Ben gets three. None is worth more than another.
steps.caption: All boxes have equal value.

steps.name: Count the whole and total parts
steps.narration: Two parts plus three parts gives five parts altogether. Those five equal parts make the full thirty pounds.
steps.caption: How many boxes altogether?

steps.name: Find the value of one part
steps.narration: Divide the total thirty pounds by five equal parts. One part is worth six pounds. Every box is worth the same six pounds.
steps.caption: Total divided by parts.

steps.name: Build the first share
steps.narration: Ava has two equal parts. Two lots of six pounds makes twelve pounds for Ava.
steps.caption: Two parts make twelve.

steps.name: Build the second share
steps.narration: Ben has three equal parts. Three lots of six pounds makes eighteen pounds for Ben.
steps.caption: Three parts make eighteen.

steps.name: Prove the total and ratio
steps.narration: Twelve pounds plus eighteen pounds gives thirty pounds. And twelve to eighteen simplifies to two to three. Both tests agree.
steps.caption: Both checks agree!

p.label: Y7-058 · Counters 6 : 9
p.context: Six blue counters to nine teal counters.

steps.name: Notice the two quantities
steps.caption: Keep the same comparison.
steps.narration: A ratio compares two quantities in order. Six blue counters and nine teal counters make a ratio of six to nine.

steps.name: Represent equal-sized bundles
steps.caption: Can we make equal bundles?
steps.narration: We can organise both collections into bundles of the same size. Each bundle must contain an equal number of counters.

steps.name: Find the common factor
steps.caption: Group both sides alike.
steps.narration: Three is a common factor of six and nine. There are two bundles on one side and three on the other.

steps.name: Collapse equal bundles
steps.caption: One bundle becomes one part.
steps.narration: Count bundles instead of individual counters. The comparison has not changed because both sides used groups of three.

steps.name: State the simplest ratio
steps.caption: Both sides change together.
steps.narration: Six to nine simplifies to two to three. Both parts were divided by the same positive common factor.

steps.name: Prove the equivalent ratio
steps.caption: Check the same multiplier.
steps.narration: Multiply both parts of two to three by three and you return to six to nine. The ratio is equivalent and the new pair has no common factor above one.

steps.name: Start with fixed area
steps.caption: Count the same area.
steps.narration: We have a rectangle made from equal square units. The area is its width multiplied by its height.

steps.name: Stretch the width
steps.caption: Wider means shorter.

steps.caption: Shorter means taller.

steps.name: Prove the constant

p.label: Y8-041 · Find the speed
p.title: A JOURNEY AT STEADY SPEED
p.context: A coach travels 90 kilometres in 1.5 hours. Find its average speed.

steps.name: See the journey
steps.caption: What do we know?
steps.narration: A journey has a distance and a time. We use these together to find its average speed.

steps.name: Watch the movement
steps.caption: Follow the route.
steps.narration: Watch the position ring move along the route. Distance grows as the journey continues.

steps.name: Measure the distance
steps.caption: Read the distance.
steps.narration: Distance tells us how far the journey travels. We measure the complete route, not just a short part.

steps.name: Measure the time
steps.caption: Read the clock.
steps.narration: Time is how long the complete journey takes. Match the distance with the same time interval.

steps.name: Choose the unknown
steps.caption: What is missing?
steps.narration: Cover the quantity you need to calculate in the formula triangle. Distance equals speed multiplied by time.

steps.name: Show the calculation
steps.caption: Use the correct units.
steps.narration: To find average speed, divide the total distance by the total time. To find distance, multiply speed by time. To find time, divide distance by speed.

steps.name: Check the answer
steps.caption: Does the journey fit?
steps.narration: Check the units and put the result back into the formula. The three quantities must agree.

p.label: Y8-028 · Graph gradient
p.title: WATER LEVEL RISING
p.context: The water rises at a steady number of centimetres each minute. Find the gradient.

steps.name: Notice the tank
steps.caption: Look at the two measurements.
steps.narration: Look at the container and the graph. We can measure how one quantity changes as another quantity increases.

steps.name: Open the tap
steps.caption: Start the flow.
steps.narration: When the flow starts, the height of the liquid begins to rise.

steps.name: Compare intervals
steps.caption: Compare equal intervals.
steps.narration: In equal time intervals, the same flow rate adds the same amount. Equal steps help us see the rate.

steps.name: Watch the depth rise
steps.caption: Follow the rising level.
steps.narration: The level climbs at a steady speed. A faster flow gives a larger change over the same time.

steps.name: Trace the graph
steps.caption: Look at the slope.
steps.narration: Put the measurements on a graph. The gradient shows how much the quantity increases for one unit along the horizontal axis.

steps.name: Calculate the rate
steps.caption: Rise divided by run.
steps.narration: Find the change on the vertical axis and divide by the change on the horizontal axis. Remember the units.

steps.name: Test a new rate
steps.caption: What if the rate doubles?
steps.narration: Keep the same horizontal interval. Doubling the rate doubles the vertical change and makes the graph steeper.

steps.name: Check the evidence
steps.caption: Both representations agree.
steps.narration: Check that the tank, graph and rate calculation all tell the same story.

p.label: Y7-059 · Sharing two to three
p.context: Ava and Ben share equal parts in the ratio 2:3.

steps.name: Notice the two-part ratio
steps.caption: First, count the groups.
steps.narration: A ratio compares parts. In two to three, the first group has two equal parts and the second has three.

steps.name: Build the one-whole bar
steps.caption: Together, they make one whole.
steps.narration: Join all the equally sized parts into one whole. Each outlined box represents exactly one equal part.

steps.name: Count the denominator
steps.caption: Count every equal box.
steps.narration: Add two and three. There are five equal parts in the whole. Five becomes the denominator for both fractions.

steps.name: Translate the first part
steps.caption: Ava has two of five.
steps.narration: The first group owns two of the five equal parts. Its fraction of the whole is two fifths, not two thirds.

steps.name: Translate the second part
steps.caption: Ben has three of five.
steps.narration: The second group owns the other three parts. Its fraction of the whole is three fifths.

steps.name: Prove the whole
steps.caption: Both fractions make one whole!
steps.narration: Two fifths plus three fifths equals five fifths, which is one whole. Both fractions use the same denominator.
